title: RetainIQ: causal retention decisioning for small subscription businesses
description:
Research software for the manuscript Reliability of Uplift Targeting and Detectability of Retention Effects at the Scale of a Small Subscription Business. An earlier version of that work was posted as a preprint under the title When Does Uplift Modelling Pay? A Correlation Criterion and a Measurement Floor for Small-Scale Subscription Retention (doi:10.5281/zenodo.22009470). Release 2.0.0 contains the code that produced the manuscript's results. It corrects or withdraws several results of release 1.0.0 and of the preprint, listed below.

The software asks what a subscription business with a few hundred to a few thousand customers can learn from its own data about whom to send a retention offer, and whether it can tell afterwards that the offer worked.

Contents:

  • A subscription simulator (SubSim) that gives, for every customer, the churn probability with and without an offer, with voluntary cancellation and failed payment as separate processes. An automated check holds its aggregate rates inside stated ranges, which were compared with published industry figures.
  • Benchmark harnesses for three public randomised experiments (Hillstrom, Criteo-UPLIFT v2.1, Lenta), analysed as four treatment-control comparisons, and for two survival datasets (Telco, GBSG2). The datasets are not redistributed; the loaders read them from their sources.
  • Small-sample reliability: how often each of five targeting methods beats random selection as the training set shrinks, over 200 draws with exact intervals.
  • The correlation between risk and response over thirty splits, on two scales and under five definitions of risk, with a diagnostic for the classifier's early stopping.
  • A Bayesian decision rule that can decline to act (Laplace posterior, checked against NUTS), and a re-implementation of the campaign-size rule of Lemmens and Gupta (2020) to compare it with.
  • A holdout module that assigns a holdout, estimates incremental retention and computes the minimum detectable effect, validated against the simulator.
  • Supporting components: a point-in-time feature store with a leakage audit, a discrete-time competing-risks survival model with Cox, random survival forest and DeepSurv baselines, an offer-ladder optimiser with reason codes, and a command-line path that checks a billing export before producing a report.

Changes since 1.0.0 that affect reported results:

  • The benchmark classifier no longer stops early. Under scikit-learn's default, the two models of a T-learner stopped at different rounds on samples just above 10,000 rows, which made one reported correlation unstable.
  • The correlation between risk and response is reported over thirty splits, with risk fitted on control customers the effect models never saw, which is the definition in Ascarza (2018). The preprint's +0.69 for one experiment came from a single split and was the highest of thirty.
  • Small-sample win rates are computed over 200 draws with intervals. The preprint's 75% and 55% came from 20 draws; the corresponding figures are 72.5% and 62.5%.
  • The claim that the correlation between risk and response is a new criterion is withdrawn. It is in Ascarza (2018).
  • The commands that compare decision rules print the corrected, money-denominated rule first. They had been printing the earlier one.

750 automated tests and four continuous-integration gates (tests, simulator calibration, leakage, and the simulator's policy comparison). The decision log records each design choice, each prediction written in advance with its outcome, and each error found.

The README lists the command that runs each analysis in the manuscript.
